REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] This is the decision in the claims for refugee protection made by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Iraq1.
DECISION

[2] The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimants left Iraq in 2001. The principal claimant worked as an engineer in Qatar and United Arab Emirates, accompanied by the associate claimant. He alleges that he lost his job, and that they cannot return to Baghdad. They state Sunni and Shia militias will target them for harm for a number of reasons including that they are moderate Sunnis, that they are educated professionals, and because of their lengthy residence outside of Iraq.
ANALYSIS

subthemes.text:
[7] The most relevant experience for assessing the forward-looking risk of the claimants is the experience of various members of the associate claimant's family, whose home was broken into in January 2017 by a militia group who physically and verbally assaulted and robbed them. While the claimants testified that a brother-in-law has moved back and forth between locations since then, various other family members have remained in the home and no further incidents have occurred. It is also unclear from the evidence, in the panel's view, whether this was for the purpose of crime (robbery) or for reasons related to sect or other factors. The lack of any continuing targeting of the family or home in the interceding two years and the lack of a clear motive for this crime leads the panel to find there to be no more than a mere possibility that the claimants' families are currently being targeted by militias in Baghdad.

[8] Recent country documentation suggests that Sunni identity alone is not sufficient to find someone faces serious harm in Baghdad:
The Upper Tribunal, in the Country Guidance case of BA (Returns to Baghdad) Iraq CG [2017] UKUT 18 (IAC), heard on 24-25 August 2016 and promulgated on 23 January 2017, found:
'Sectarian violence has increased since the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces in 2012, but is not at the levels seen in 2006-2007. A Shia dominated government is supported by Shia militias in Baghdad. The evidence indicates that Sunni men are more likely to be targeted as suspected supporters of Sunni extremist groups such as ISIL [Daesh]. However, Sunni identity alone is not sufficient to give rise to a real risk of serious harm' (paragraph 107, (v)).
'Individual characteristics, which do not in themselves create a real risk of serious harm on return to Baghdad might amount to a real risk for the purpose of the Refugee Convention, Article 15(c) of the Qualification Directive or Article 3 of the ECHR [European Convention on Human Rights] if assessed on a cumulative basis. The assessment will depend on the facts of each case' (paragraph 107 (vi)).2

[9] A similar sentiment is found in another recent document3:
Sunnis
Sunnis' removal from their privileged position under the Ba'ath Party regime resulted in many feeling excluded and marginalised. This has been further exacerbated by the perceived association of the Sunni community with ISIL and the limited capacity of the Government to assist Sunnis attempting to flee ISIL, who have been disproportionately affected by the current conflict. While the Government has worked hard to protect civilians in the fight against ISIL, it has at times failed to respond firmly to acts of retribution by the Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) or the PMF. These factors have intensified tensions between Sunni and Shia communities in Iraq.
Sunnis are active and present in the Government and the bureaucracy. Some Provincial Governors (including the Governors of Anbar and Ninewa provinces) are Sunni. Despite this, the implementation of non-discriminatory legislation is often subject to societal prejudice against Sunnis.
While in part related to the fight against ISIL, in-country contacts report that some Sunnis continue to be systematically harassed, accused of supporting ISIL and physically harmed by PMF groups and, to a lesser extent, other parts of the ISF in some areas. This includes reports of abuses of Sunni males when trying to flee ISIL controlled areas as well as Sunnis being prevented from leaving and entering Government controlled areas. For example, the US Department of State's Human Rights Reports in 2016 highlighted multiple NGO reports of more than 643 men and boys being reported missing following the June 2016 liberation of Fallujah after they were intercepted by PMF groups at ad hoc security sites. All 643 men and boys reportedly remain missing. Looting and destruction of Sunni owned properties following the liberation of ISIL-controlled areas is also occurring on occasion and, in some areas, displaced Sunnis are being prevented from returning to their homes. Outside of ISIL-controlled areas, Sunnis have claimed they face harassment and discrimination, including through undergoing more intrusive inspections at checkpoints and the provision of poorer quality services in Sunni areas.
Intra-Sunni tensions exist, including between those who support ISIL and others who resist ISIL. In-country contacts report that the Sunni community and, in particular, the Sunni leadership is divided. Intra-Sunni militia and tribal violence occurs.
Overall, DFAT assesses that official and societal discrimination and violence towards Sunnis is increasing and tolerance for Sunnis in non-Sunni areas has declined. Sunnis located in non-Sunni areas (such as Shia areas of Baghdad and the south) face a high level of societal discrimination and violence. In Sunni areas, the risk is lower. However, in ISIL-controlled areas, Sunnis who refuse to support ISIL face a high risk of discrimination and violence.

[10] The panel finds that simply being Sunni in Baghdad, particularly if living in a Sunni-majority area is likely to lead to discrimination and harassment, but violence against Sunnis is not so widespread that there is more than a mere possibility of facing serious harm.
Risk as moderate Sunnis

[11] The claimants allege there are several factors that lead them to be at greater risk, even in Sunni areas of Baghdad. The first of these is their religion as moderate Sunnis.

[12] When asked what makes them moderate, the principal claimant explained that they respect others and do not discriminate, and that their religious practice is not hard-line. They noted that the female claimant wears a hijab, not a niqab or other heavy covering and the principal claimant did not have a beard. The claimants do attend mosque but with a frequency that would signify them as moderate.

[13] The panel finds that, while the claimants describe themselves as moderate, their actions and activities are not likely to attract the attention of militias such that they would face harm as alleged. Simply not discriminating against other religions and attending mosque on a regular rather than frequent basis, and wearing moderate attire (hijab, no beard) is not described in the documentation as being problematic for persons in Baghdad. The claimants appear to be regular practicing Muslims, and are not taking actions to disrupt religious norms or activities. As thus, their "moderate" religious beliefs and activities would not, in the panel's view, result in them facing a serious possibility of persecution.
Risk as Engineers

[14] While the associate claimant did go to university, according to her intake forms, she has not been working as a professional for at least ten years4. As such, the panel finds it unlikely that she would be targeted as a professional or woman professional.

[15] The male claimant stopped working when he came to Canada. He is sixty-nine years old. He testified that he does not have a pension and would have to work as an engineer in Iraq, putting him at risk. The panel has concerns about the credibility of this statement. The claimant has been working, according to him, in a professional capacity for fourty-five years, and in the Gulf for over fifteen years. There is no indication that he is anything other than a responsible, professional individual. He has obtained numerous visas and engaged in international travel5. The panel finds it unlikely that he did not make plans to care for himself and his spouse financially in his later years, despite his assertions that he would need to work for financial reasons. Further, while the claimant and his counsel allege he would have to work as an engineer, this is not supported by evidence. There is no known requirement for engineers to work in this field. The panel finds that the evidence does not support that the principal claimant would have to work in Iraq as an engineer, and face targeting as a professional as a result. If he did have to work, he could engage in other work.

[16] The panel finds that the documentary evidence does not support that retired or former professionals that have left the fields for upwards of a year continue to be targeted.
Risk related to time overseas

[17] The claimants allege that they will be at risk because of the time they have spent in Qatar and U.A.E. as well as now Canada. This relates, according to testimony, to the appearance of wealth, and higher likelihood of being targeted (primarily for theft, extortion or kidnapping). First, the panel finds there is not a link to the Convention on this ground. The claimants are describing a fear of being victims of crime as a result of perceived wealth. This is well established as a type of claim that does not hold a nexus to the Convention.

[18] Further, the panel finds the evidence does not establish that those who have been outside the country, primarily in the Gulf, are subject to such levels of violence that there would be a serious possibility the claimants would be so targeted upon return.

[19] Counsel cited item 1.24 of the national documentation package for Iraq to suggest that persons such as the claimants would be at risk of harm upon return - however, this item relates to the situation of perceived collaborators6. It does not suggest that anyone who has lived in the Gulf or for some time in the West would be seen in this light. Nor does it support that perceived collaborators are broadly at risk in Iraq, stating "no real risk based on being perceived as a collaborator". Further cited was item 1.7 which states that Shia groups do target persons for extortion7. This item is from 2012, and does not state that these groups target returnees such as the claimants.

The panel does not find in the documents evidence that persons returning from working abroad are subject to harm.
The claimant did use English occasionally in the hearing - when responding to a question posed to him in English by the panel.
The panel sees no reports of persons who have spoken a few words of English being targeted for harm as a result in the recent documentary evidence.
He testified that he uses English professionally, however, as noted above, the panel is not satisfied that the claimant would return to his professional work.

subthemes.text:
[20] The general country documentation supports that Iraq has long been subject to economic and security issues, and as such it is not uncommon for Iraqis to have left Iraq to work or live abroad for periods of time. The panel does not find in the documents evidence that persons returning from working abroad are subject to harm. Were this to be the case, given the large number of persons who have left the country, it would expect this to be reported. This lack of evidence is indicative, to the panel, that such persons are not subject to a well-founded risk of persecution or a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.
Use of English

[21] The counsel suggests that the principal claimant speaks English and may "slip" and use English if he were to return to Iraq, which would then lead to him being targeted for harm. The claimant did use English occasionally in the hearing - when responding to a question posed to him in English by the panel. This does not, in the panel's view, suggest that if he were speaking Arabic in Iraq to other Iraqis he would do something similar. He testified that he uses English professionally, however, as noted above, the panel is not satisfied that the claimant would return to his professional work. However, even if he were to use English on occasion in Iraq, simply speaking the language is not supported as a cause of harm for individuals in the country. The panel sees no reports of persons who have spoken a few words of English being targeted for harm as a result in the recent documentary evidence.
Risk due to Gender

argument_evidence.context_text: The panel further considered whether she would be at risk as a woman and finds this not to be the case.
[22] The panel earlier considered the evidence and found that the female claimant is not likely to be seen as a professional, nor as so moderate as to be problematic.

The panel finds that the evidence supports that women who enjoy the support of family members in Iraq and are not subject to targeted violence (such as domestic violence or because of other factors such as political profile) are not particularly vulnerable to the types of violence that some women face in Iraq8, such that they do not face a serious possibility of persecution nor do they face a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture on a balance of probabilities.

[22] The panel earlier considered the evidence and found that the female claimant is not likely to be seen as a professional, nor as so moderate as to be problematic. The panel further considered whether she would be at risk as a woman and finds this not to be the case. The associate (female) claimant is a married woman with the support of her spouse. The panel finds that the evidence supports that women who enjoy the support of family members in Iraq and are not subject to targeted violence (such as domestic violence or because of other factors such as political profile) are not particularly vulnerable to the types of violence that some women face in Iraq8, such that they do not face a serious possibility of persecution nor do they face a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture on a balance of probabilities.

The panel finds that the evidence supports that women who enjoy the support of family members in Iraq and are not subject to targeted violence (such as domestic violence or because of other factors such as political profile) are not particularly vulnerable to the types of violence that some women face in Iraq8, such that they do not face a serious possibility of persecution nor do they face a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture on a balance of probabilities.

REASONS FOR DECISION

[1] This is the decision in the claims for refugee protection made by XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX and XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX, citizens of Iraq1.
DECISION

[2] The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
ALLEGATIONS

[3] The claimants left Iraq in 2001. The principal claimant worked as an engineer in Qatar and United Arab Emirates, accompanied by the associate claimant. He alleges that he lost his job, and that they cannot return to Baghdad. They state Sunni and Shia militias will target them for harm for a number of reasons including that they are moderate Sunnis, that they are educated professionals, and because of their lengthy residence outside of Iraq.
ANALYSIS

[4] The main issues in the claims were credibility and whether the objective evidence supports that the claimants face a serious possibility of persecution or a risk to their life, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger or torture on a balance of probabilities. There is also an issue of nexus to the Convention related to the risk they allege related to their residence outside of Iraq.
Risk as Sunnis

[5] The claimants allege they would be at risk as moderate Sunnis. The panel believes the claimants are Sunni as alleged. The claimants' families remaining in Iraq live in predominantly Sunni neighbourhoods of Baghdad, and this is likely where the claimants would live should they return to Baghdad.

[6] They outlined several experiences of family members in Iraq in their BOCs and in testimony, most that can be distinguished from the claimants, such as the cousin who was killed in what appeared to have been an attempt on the life of another family member who was a candidate for election in 2010 (the claimants have no known political profile), and a nephew targeted in 2004 (many years ago, as a young man, unlike the claimants).

[7] The most relevant experience for assessing the forward-looking risk of the claimants is the experience of various members of the associate claimant's family, whose home was broken into in January 2017 by a militia group who physically and verbally assaulted and robbed them. While the claimants testified that a brother-in-law has moved back and forth between locations since then, various other family members have remained in the home and no further incidents have occurred. It is also unclear from the evidence, in the panel's view, whether this was for the purpose of crime (robbery) or for reasons related to sect or other factors. The lack of any continuing targeting of the family or home in the interceding two years and the lack of a clear motive for this crime leads the panel to find there to be no more than a mere possibility that the claimants' families are currently being targeted by militias in Baghdad.

[8] Recent country documentation suggests that Sunni identity alone is not sufficient to find someone faces serious harm in Baghdad:
The Upper Tribunal, in the Country Guidance case of BA (Returns to Baghdad) Iraq CG [2017] UKUT 18 (IAC), heard on 24-25 August 2016 and promulgated on 23 January 2017, found:
'Sectarian violence has increased since the withdrawal of US-led coalition forces in 2012, but is not at the levels seen in 2006-2007. A Shia dominated government is supported by Shia militias in Baghdad. The evidence indicates that Sunni men are more likely to be targeted as suspected supporters of Sunni extremist groups such as ISIL [Daesh]. However, Sunni identity alone is not sufficient to give rise to a real risk of serious harm' (paragraph 107, (v)).
'Individual characteristics, which do not in themselves create a real risk of serious harm on return to Baghdad might amount to a real risk for the purpose of the Refugee Convention, Article 15(c) of the Qualification Directive or Article 3 of the ECHR [European Convention on Human Rights] if assessed on a cumulative basis. The assessment will depend on the facts of each case' (paragraph 107 (vi)).2

[9] A similar sentiment is found in another recent document3:
Sunnis
Sunnis' removal from their privileged position under the Ba'ath Party regime resulted in many feeling excluded and marginalised. This has been further exacerbated by the perceived association of the Sunni community with ISIL and the limited capacity of the Government to assist Sunnis attempting to flee ISIL, who have been disproportionately affected by the current conflict. While the Government has worked hard to protect civilians in the fight against ISIL, it has at times failed to respond firmly to acts of retribution by the Iraqi Security Forces (ISF) or the PMF. These factors have intensified tensions between Sunni and Shia communities in Iraq.
Sunnis are active and present in the Government and the bureaucracy. Some Provincial Governors (including the Governors of Anbar and Ninewa provinces) are Sunni. Despite this, the implementation of non-discriminatory legislation is often subject to societal prejudice against Sunnis.
While in part related to the fight against ISIL, in-country contacts report that some Sunnis continue to be systematically harassed, accused of supporting ISIL and physically harmed by PMF groups and, to a lesser extent, other parts of the ISF in some areas. This includes reports of abuses of Sunni males when trying to flee ISIL controlled areas as well as Sunnis being prevented from leaving and entering Government controlled areas. For example, the US Department of State's Human Rights Reports in 2016 highlighted multiple NGO reports of more than 643 men and boys being reported missing following the June 2016 liberation of Fallujah after they were intercepted by PMF groups at ad hoc security sites. All 643 men and boys reportedly remain missing. Looting and destruction of Sunni owned properties following the liberation of ISIL-controlled areas is also occurring on occasion and, in some areas, displaced Sunnis are being prevented from returning to their homes. Outside of ISIL-controlled areas, Sunnis have claimed they face harassment and discrimination, including through undergoing more intrusive inspections at checkpoints and the provision of poorer quality services in Sunni areas.
Intra-Sunni tensions exist, including between those who support ISIL and others who resist ISIL. In-country contacts report that the Sunni community and, in particular, the Sunni leadership is divided. Intra-Sunni militia and tribal violence occurs.
Overall, DFAT assesses that official and societal discrimination and violence towards Sunnis is increasing and tolerance for Sunnis in non-Sunni areas has declined. Sunnis located in non-Sunni areas (such as Shia areas of Baghdad and the south) face a high level of societal discrimination and violence. In Sunni areas, the risk is lower. However, in ISIL-controlled areas, Sunnis who refuse to support ISIL face a high risk of discrimination and violence.

[10] The panel finds that simply being Sunni in Baghdad, particularly if living in a Sunni-majority area is likely to lead to discrimination and harassment, but violence against Sunnis is not so widespread that there is more than a mere possibility of facing serious harm.
Risk as moderate Sunnis
[11] The claimants allege there are several factors that lead them to be at greater risk, even in Sunni areas of Baghdad. The first of these is their religion as moderate Sunnis.

[12] When asked what makes them moderate, the principal claimant explained that they respect others and do not discriminate, and that their religious practice is not hard-line. They noted that the female claimant wears a hijab, not a niqab or other heavy covering and the principal claimant did not have a beard. The claimants do attend mosque but with a frequency that would signify them as moderate.

[13] The panel finds that, while the claimants describe themselves as moderate, their actions and activities are not likely to attract the attention of militias such that they would face harm as alleged. Simply not discriminating against other religions and attending mosque on a regular rather than frequent basis, and wearing moderate attire (hijab, no beard) is not described in the documentation as being problematic for persons in Baghdad. The claimants appear to be regular practicing Muslims, and are not taking actions to disrupt religious norms or activities. As thus, their "moderate" religious beliefs and activities would not, in the panel's view, result in them facing a serious possibility of persecution.
Risk as Engineers

[14] While the associate claimant did go to university, according to her intake forms, she has not been working as a professional for at least ten years4. As such, the panel finds it unlikely that she would be targeted as a professional or woman professional.

[15] The male claimant stopped working when he came to Canada. He is sixty-nine years old. He testified that he does not have a pension and would have to work as an engineer in Iraq, putting him at risk. The panel has concerns about the credibility of this statement. The claimant has been working, according to him, in a professional capacity for fourty-five years, and in the Gulf for over fifteen years. There is no indication that he is anything other than a responsible, professional individual. He has obtained numerous visas and engaged in international travel5. The panel finds it unlikely that he did not make plans to care for himself and his spouse financially in his later years, despite his assertions that he would need to work for financial reasons. Further, while the claimant and his counsel allege he would have to work as an engineer, this is not supported by evidence. There is no known requirement for engineers to work in this field. The panel finds that the evidence does not support that the principal claimant would have to work in Iraq as an engineer, and face targeting as a professional as a result. If he did have to work, he could engage in other work.

[16] The panel finds that the documentary evidence does not support that retired or former professionals that have left the fields for upwards of a year continue to be targeted.
Risk related to time overseas

[17] The claimants allege that they will be at risk because of the time they have spent in Qatar and U.A.E. as well as now Canada. This relates, according to testimony, to the appearance of wealth, and higher likelihood of being targeted (primarily for theft, extortion or kidnapping). First, the panel finds there is not a link to the Convention on this ground. The claimants are describing a fear of being victims of crime as a result of perceived wealth. This is well established as a type of claim that does not hold a nexus to the Convention.

[18] Further, the panel finds the evidence does not establish that those who have been outside the country, primarily in the Gulf, are subject to such levels of violence that there would be a serious possibility the claimants would be so targeted upon return.

[19] Counsel cited item 1.24 of the national documentation package for Iraq to suggest that persons such as the claimants would be at risk of harm upon return - however, this item relates to the situation of perceived collaborators6. It does not suggest that anyone who has lived in the Gulf or for some time in the West would be seen in this light. Nor does it support that perceived collaborators are broadly at risk in Iraq, stating "no real risk based on being perceived as a collaborator". Further cited was item 1.7 which states that Shia groups do target persons for extortion7. This item is from 2012, and does not state that these groups target returnees such as the claimants.

[20] The general country documentation supports that Iraq has long been subject to economic and security issues, and as such it is not uncommon for Iraqis to have left Iraq to work or live abroad for periods of time. The panel does not find in the documents evidence that persons returning from working abroad are subject to harm. Were this to be the case, given the large number of persons who have left the country, it would expect this to be reported. This lack of evidence is indicative, to the panel, that such persons are not subject to a well-founded risk of persecution or a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture.
Use of English

[21] The counsel suggests that the principal claimant speaks English and may "slip" and use English if he were to return to Iraq, which would then lead to him being targeted for harm. The claimant did use English occasionally in the hearing - when responding to a question posed to him in English by the panel. This does not, in the panel's view, suggest that if he were speaking Arabic in Iraq to other Iraqis he would do something similar. He testified that he uses English professionally, however, as noted above, the panel is not satisfied that the claimant would return to his professional work. However, even if he were to use English on occasion in Iraq, simply speaking the language is not supported as a cause of harm for individuals in the country. The panel sees no reports of persons who have spoken a few words of English being targeted for harm as a result in the recent documentary evidence.
Risk due to Gender

[22] The panel earlier considered the evidence and found that the female claimant is not likely to be seen as a professional, nor as so moderate as to be problematic. The panel further considered whether she would be at risk as a woman and finds this not to be the case. The associate (female) claimant is a married woman with the support of her spouse. The panel finds that the evidence supports that women who enjoy the support of family members in Iraq and are not subject to targeted violence (such as domestic violence or because of other factors such as political profile) are not particularly vulnerable to the types of violence that some women face in Iraq8, such that they do not face a serious possibility of persecution nor do they face a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture on a balance of probabilities.
Cumulative risk

[23] The panel further considered whether, when considered cumulatively, the above-noted factors would result in the claimants facing a serious possibility of persecution, and finds they do not. In regards to many of the factors, the panel found that the evidence simply did not support that those with that profile are at risk in Iraq. For the remaining, the level of risk was so minimal as to find it does not, either individually or cumulatively, result in a finding that the claimants face a serious possibility of facing persecution in Iraq. Likewise, they do not face a risk to their lives, risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture should they return to Iraq.
CONCLUSION

[24] While the panel sympathises with the claimants' stated fear of returning to Iraq after being outside of the country for a very lengthy period, particularly with no children remaining there to support them as they age, it finds the documentary and personal evidence does not support that they face a serious possibility of persecution in the country, nor do they face a risk to their lives, a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a danger of torture on a balance of probabilities.
[25] The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

[26] The claims are rejected.
(signed)
"K. Pike"
K. Pike
February 12, 2019
